one_liner: Zig port of simdjson with streaming and reflection decoding; its On-Demand parser beats simdjson on 3 of 5 author benchmarks.
what_it_does: A Zig reimplementation of simdjson's two-stage SIMD JSON parser. It offers simdjson-style DOM and On-Demand APIs in two variants: FullParser, which holds a document of up to 4 GiB in memory, and StreamParser, which pulls from a std.io.AnyReader in 64 KiB chunks and keeps memory constant for any document size. It adds a Serde-like decoder driven by comptime reflection (`document.as(T, allocator, .{})`) that supports field renaming, union representations and handling of unknown fields. It ships as a Zig package (`zig fetch`) and exports no C ABI, so C++ code cannot use it in place of simdjson.
how_it_is_fast: Stage 1 follows the Langdale-Lemire simdjson design. It classifies characters with nibble-lookup shuffles (inline vpshufb on x86-64, tbl on AArch64). It finds string spans by applying a carry-less-multiply prefix-XOR (vpclmulqdq) to the quote mask, plus odd/even backslash-run arithmetic. It then extracts structural positions into a u32 index with tzcnt/clz loops, processing two 64-byte masks per iteration on x86. On-Demand walks that index lazily and parses only the values you access; the number parser sits in modules named eisel_lemire, digit_comp and BigInt. StreamParser keeps the bytes and a u16/u32 chunk-relative index in mirrored ring buffers (memfd+mmap on POSIX, VirtualAlloc2 placeholders on Windows), which is how memory stays constant.
when_to_use: A Zig program that pulls a few fields out of large JSON (hundreds of MB, such as the 626 MB EDSM systemsPopulated dump) and wants simdjson On-Demand behaviour without C++ interop.
A single JSON document too large to hold in memory, or over 4 GiB: StreamParser parses it with constant memory. The README lists this as a feature zimdjson adds on top of simdjson.

Decoding a known schema into Zig structs. In the author's twitter.json chart, Schema mode runs at ~1.07 GB/s, compared with ~0.83 GB/s for serde_json::from_str and ~0.33 GB/s for std.json.parseFromSlice.
Builds you control that target x86-64 with AVX/PCLMUL or AArch64, on Linux, macOS or Windows.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ codebases: use simdjson directly. In the author's own chart, simdjson won both twitter.json On-Demand tasks (~2.84 vs ~2.64 and ~2.82 vs ~2.43 GB/s) and all five DOM tasks (for example find-system ~0.90 vs ~0.80 GB/s).
Projects on Zig 0.15 or 0.16. main pins Zig 0.14.0 and its API is built on std.io.AnyReader. PR #11 reports that the 0.15.x branch still fails on 0.15.2, and the 0.16 port (PR #13) is unmerged.

Reading On-Demand fields in a different order from the document. The author's schema chart shows 'On-Demand, Unordered' at ~0.23 GB/s, slower than std.json. The README suggests switching to schema mode to avoid this.

Binaries that must run on unknown CPUs. SIMD features are fixed at compile time: there is no runtime dispatch (issue #4) and no scalar fallback (issue #3), targets without SIMD fail with a compile error, and architectures other than x86-64 and AArch64 hit @compileError.
Code that needs an active upstream. The last commit on main is from 2025-04-29 and the last tag, 0.1.1, is from 2025-03-23.

integration.dependencies: None at runtime (Zig std only). simdjson v3.10.1, yyjson 0.10.0, a RapidJSON fork and test-data archives are lazy dependencies used only by the benchmarks and tests.
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.14.0 (minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon; CI pins 0.14.0). Newer Zig versions need the unmerged 0.15.x branch or community PRs.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (streaming needs Windows 10 or later). CPUs: x86-64 with AVX and PCLMULQDQ (VEX-encoded inline asm) or AArch64 (NEON tbl). Vector width comes from the compile target.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Each parser owns its buffers and handles one document at a time, and the docs say to use several parser instances for several documents. There is no internal multithreading (issue #5 is open).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it mirrors simdjson's On-Demand and DOM ideas: in the paired benchmark code, at()/atOrdered() stand in for simdjson's operator[], and it also has getArraySize and raw strings. But it is a Zig-only API with no C/C++ ABI, so moving to it means rewriting call sites in Zig.

gotchas: On-Demand checks only the parts of the document you read ('validate what you use'), so malformed JSON can parse without error. The OutOfOrderIteration misuse check exists only in Debug builds, so release builds do not report out-of-order access.

StreamParser returns error.StreamChunkOverflow in three cases: a string or number longer than the chunk (64 KiB by default), a whitespace run longer than the chunk, or a rewind past the current chunk. RawString values become invalid when the chunk advances, and asString results become invalid on the next parse. On macOS each ring buffer is asserted to be at most 4 MiB, which limits chunk_length.

The README's install line pins tag 0.1.1 (2025-03-23). That tag predates the fix for issue #8, where large structs in schema mode exceed the comptime backward-branch quota. The fix exists only on main (commit aa22af4).

The benchmark harness is not symmetric. For On-Demand, simdjson calls padded_string::load inside every timed run, allocating a new buffer each time, while zimdjson reuses a buffer pre-sized with expectDocumentSize. For DOM, simdjson uses parser.load. zimdjson DOM loses to simdjson DOM on all five tasks, so part of the ~1.5x On-Demand win on the 626 MB file may come from buffer allocation rather than parsing. This was not measured separately.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zimdjson over simdjson only when your code is Zig or you need constant-memory streaming of one huge document. Pick it over yyjson when you touch only a few fields: in the author's chart, yyjson ran at 0.46-1.72 GB/s and zimdjson On-Demand at 1.59-2.64 GB/s. For Rust or C++, simd-json, simdjson, yyjson or glaze are the natural choices.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran their own Linux perf_event harness on a 3.30 GHz Skylake (model not given), with every contender built by `zig build --release=fast` (ReleaseFast, per scripts/bench_ondemand.py). simdjson v3.10.1 was compiled with Zig's bundled Clang, and the Zig version is not recorded. zimdjson's On-Demand FullParser beat simdjson On-Demand by about 1.5x on three extraction tasks over the 626 MB systemsPopulated.json (find-system ~1.74 vs ~1.17 GB/s, for example) but lost both twitter.json tasks. Throughput is file size divided by the mean wall time, including reading the file, over at least 3 runs and up to 10 s.
status_note: Stale: main was last touched on 2025-04-29 and the last tag is 0.1.1 (2025-03-23); Zig 0.15 and 0.16 ports sit in an unmerged branch and in community PRs. It is MIT-licensed pure Zig, so the practical path is to vendor it and pin Zig 0.14.
